page: Vultr vx1-m-16c-128g-960s is a memory-optimized server instance belonging to the VX1 Cloud Compute family. It features 16 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 8 physical AMD EPYC cores with multithreading enabled. The system is equipped with 128.0 GB of RAM, providing a high memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per core. Local storage consists of a bundled 960 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU hardware is present on this configuration.

Performance benchmarks indicate strong single-core capabilities, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance, single-threaded gzip compression, and single-threaded bzip3 decompression all ranking in the top tier. Multi-core CPU performance, multi-threaded bzip3 decompression, and Passmark CPU scores fall within the average range. Memory performance is robust, with a Passmark memory score in the top 25%, while memory bandwidth read and write operations remain average. For machine learning workloads, the instance achieves top-tier text generation speeds and strong prompt processing speeds on small 135M models, though performance scales down to average on medium 7B models.

This instance offers a balanced qualitative cost-efficiency profile for memory-intensive workloads, providing a high density of RAM and dedicated AMD EPYC compute resources without the premium of GPU accelerators. The combination of dedicated CPU allocation, high memory capacity, and fast local NVMe SSD storage makes this server well-suited for database operations, memory-cached web serving, and moderate-scale data processing tasks.

Operating on the x86_64 architecture, this instance delivers top-tier single-core CPU performance and strong memory scores, alongside average multi-core and memory bandwidth capabilities. With a high memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB per core and dedicated CPU allocation, it provides a cost-effective resource profile for workloads requiring significant memory capacity without GPU acceleration. It is highly suited for database hosting, caching layers, and memory-intensive enterprise applications.
